imageCaption: A kitchen counter splits down the middle—one side shows plantains being peeled and mashed, the other side shows the same plantains already transformed into golden mofongo, with both versions existing simultaneously as Sully watches from beneath the table
text:
Aaliyah was halfway through the third plantain when the kitchen decided to exist in two moments at once.

It wasn't dramatic. It was the opposite of dramatic. It was so ordinary that she almost didn't notice it—the way her hands were simultaneously pressing the plantain into the bowl and the mofongo was already golden and steaming, ready to serve. The way the timer on the stove was showing both three minutes and thirty seconds remaining.

Sully barked three times from under the table. Not panicked. Observational.

Minor glitch nearby.

"Oh," Aaliyah said, staring at her hands. They were in the process of mashing. They were also done mashing. Both were completely real. "Is this—are we—"

"The Saturday Superposition," Luisana said calmly from the doorway, where she'd appeared with Marco and three bags of plantains that had cost significantly more than plantains should cost, which meant they were the right plantains. "The kitchen is showing us both versions of what happens. What we do now and what we'll have done."

Marco stepped forward with the kind of confidence that came from watching a timeline fragment in front of you at least monthly. He surveyed the dual-state kitchen with the precision of someone examining a chess board where both sets of moves had already been played.

"This is a good glitch," he said finally. "This is the neighborhood blessing the recipe before the neighborhood blesses the recipe. The timeline is so sure this mofongo matters that it's showing up twice. It's like when an old record skips the good part because the needle loves it too much to move on."

Anthony, who had been elbow-deep in garlic prep, looked up. His expression shifted through surprise, understanding, and then something that looked a lot like being moved to tears by a glitching timeline.

"The house is telling us it's going to work," he said quietly.

"Not the house," Marco corrected. "The neighborhood. The street. The people who've been waiting for your family to stop running and start building. They want this mofongo. They want it so badly that time itself is showing up early to taste it."

Elijah chose this moment to arrive with a bag of coconut that he'd somehow convinced Marco to buy even though nobody had asked for it. He took in the kitchen in its dual state with zero surprise. "Oh good," he said. "We're cooking in both directions now. That's probably fine. Sully seems to think it's fine."

Sully, for his part, appeared to be taking notes on the dual-state plantains with the seriousness of a critic evaluating competing restaurants.

"What do we do?" Aaliyah asked. She could feel her scientific mind trying to categorize this, to understand the mechanics. But underneath the categorization was something else—the realization that her family's entire journey had been leading to a moment where a timeline would split itself down the middle just to celebrate a recipe that shouldn't work but did.

"You finish," Marco said. "You finish both versions. You complete the moment that's trying to happen. The kitchen is showing you the recipe works by showing you it's already finished. You just have to catch up."

So they did.

Aaliyah's hands moved with a certainty that felt almost like memory—like she'd already done this and was now doing it again, which was, technically, exactly what was happening. She pressed the plantain mash into the bowl. She folded in the tamarind. She poured the broth infused with coconut and lime. She drizzled the honey in a pattern that seemed to matter, though she couldn't have explained why.

The glitch didn't resolve. Both versions persisted—the cooking version and the finished version, existing side by side like a before-and-after that was happening at exactly the same time.

"What happens when we close the loop?" Aaliyah asked. "When one version catches up to the other?"

"They merge," Marco said. "Two truths become one truth. But it's a stronger truth because two timelines had to agree on it first."

Luisana was writing in her journal, her hand moving fast. Aaliyah caught glimpses: *The kitchen split down the middle. The mofongo blessed itself. The neighborhood whispered yes.*

Anthony had his phone out—not to take a picture, but to record audio. Capturing the exact moment the kitchen sounded like two kitchens. The scrape of the spoon, the simmer of the broth, the almost imperceptible sound of a timeline recognizing itself.

"Okay," Aaliyah said, and she picked up the finished mofongo from the version that had already succeeded. She held it directly above the bowl she was still preparing. "I'm going to trust the glitch."

And she pressed both versions together.

There was a moment—just barely a moment, not even long enough to be called a flicker—where the kitchen existed in every possible state at once. Where both timelines were equally real and equally true. Where the mofongo was cooking and finished and tasting like home and tasting like traveling and tasting like the thing that would finally convince a neighborhood that the Gomez family wasn't just visiting anymore.

Then it solidified.

One bowl. One perfect mofongo. One recipe that tasted like chaos made intentional.

The kitchen was completely still. The timer showed zero. The stove was empty. There was a pressed morpho butterfly sitting on top of the finished dish—Abuela Ida checking in, Marco would later say, making sure her granddaughter's chaotic recipe was going to make the neighborhood cry the right way.

"That," Elijah said with absolute certainty, "is going to change everything."

And nobody told him he was wrong, because they all felt it too—the weight of a timeline that had bent itself to acknowledge that some recipes matter enough to exist in two places at once.

Aaliyah looked at her family around the kitchen: her father grinning like he'd just watched his daughter accidentally invent the future, her mother writing down every detail, her brother already planning which neighbor should try it first, her dog who had known this was going to happen before any of them did.

"We should probably get this to Marco's before it cools down," she said softly.

"It won't cool down," Marco said. "Not this one. This one will stay warm until someone loves it."

And Aaliyah understood, holding the bowl that two timelines had had to agree on, that the neighborhood had already started.
